Empirical Research Plan  
“Economic and Environmental Effects of the Southern California NOx Trading Program”

------------------------------------------------
1. Identification Strategy
------------------------------------------------
Choice: Difference-in-differences (DID) complemented by an event-study with firm and year fixed effects.

Justification  
• The RECLAIM/NOx Trading Program was introduced at a well-defined moment (1994) and applies only to a subset of emitters.  
• We have an unbalanced panel of firms observed for several years pre- and post-policy, allowing us to compare treated and untreated firms over time.  
• We can test the parallel-trends assumption graphically and formally via the event-study coefficients.  
• An IV or RDD is not natural here: no sharp running variable at the adoption margin, and permit prices are endogenous.

------------------------------------------------
2. Treatment and Control
------------------------------------------------
Treatment variable  
Treated = 1 if firm is legally covered by the Southern California NOx cap-and-trade program (large stationary sources >4 tons/year of NOx), 0 otherwise.

Control group (counterfactual)  
Preferred: Southern California firms in similar industries that (i) fall below the RECLAIM size threshold or (ii) operate processes exempt from the rule (e.g., small boilers, emergency generators).  
Alternative robustness controls:  
  – Similar-sized emitters in Northern California (outside RECLAIM jurisdiction).  
  – Synthetic control constructed from the U.S. EPA’s Air Markets Program Data (AMPD).

Treatment timing  
policy_year = 1994.  
post_it = 1 for years ≥ 1994, 0 otherwise.

Event-study specification: leads/lags from t = –5 to t = +10.

------------------------------------------------
3. Key Identifying Assumptions
------------------------------------------------
A1. Parallel pre-treatment trends: In the absence of RECLAIM, treated and control firms would have experienced similar NOx emissions, revenues, and employment trajectories.  
• Plausibility: Both groups operate in the same regional economy and face identical state/federal regulations, making similar trends reasonable.

A2. No spillovers/interference: Control firms’ outcomes are not influenced by the trading program (e.g., through input-output links or local air-quality improvements).  
• Plausibility: Some spillovers are possible via cleaner air or permit markets; we will address with spatial buffers and industry-by-year fixed effects.

A3. Stable unit composition: Treatment status is fixed; firms do not manipulate size just before 1994 to avoid coverage.  
• Plausibility: Size threshold manipulation is unlikely on short notice; we can test for bunching around the cutoff.

A4. No other simultaneous policy shocks differentially affecting treated firms in 1994.  
• Plausibility: We will verify by reviewing EPA rules and California state policies for concurrent changes.

------------------------------------------------
4. Threats to Identification & Mitigation
------------------------------------------------
T1. Differential economic shocks (e.g., defense contraction in aerospace industry).  
• Mitigation: Industry-by-year fixed effects; control for firm-specific trends; placebo tests in pre-period.

T2. Selection into treatment (large emitters differ systematically).  
• Mitigation: Propensity-score weighting to balance observables; triple-difference using a size-based cutoff; matching + DID.

T3. Permit trading spillovers improve regional air quality for everyone, contaminating controls.  
• Mitigation: Use geographically distant controls (Northern CA) or industry controls outside the South Coast AQMD; run spatial DID excluding control firms within 30 km of treated plants.

------------------------------------------------
5. R Code Outline
------------------------------------------------
```r
# 0. Packages
library(data.table)
library(fixest)
library(did)        # Callaway–Sant’Anna for staggered timing if needed
library(ggplot2)

# 1. Load data
df <- fread("nox_reclaim_firm_level.csv")   # assume panel data

# 2. Variable construction
df[, post := (year >= 1994)]
df[, treat := (covered_by_RECLAIM == 1)]    # indicator in raw data
df[, did := treat * post]

# Balance check / summary
summary(df[, .(n_firms = uniqueN(firm_id)), by = .(treat)])

# 3. Main DID specification
# Outcome 1: log NOx emissions
did_nox <- feols(log(nox_emissions + 1) ~ did + log(employment + 1) | 
                 firm_id + year, cluster = ~firm_id, data = df)

# Outcome 2: log firm revenue
did_rev <- feols(log(revenue + 1) ~ did + log(employment + 1) |
                 firm_id + year, cluster = ~firm_id, data = df)

# 4. Event-study (leads/lags up to 5 years pre, 10 years post)
df[, rel_year := year - 1994]
# restrict window
df <- df[rel_year %between% c(-5,10)]
event <- feols(log(nox_emissions + 1) ~ i(rel_year, treat, ref = -1) + 
               log(employment + 1) | firm_id + year,
               cluster=~firm_id, data = df)
iplot(event) + geom_vline(xintercept = 0, lty=2)

# 5. Robustness: Propensity score weighting + DID
#   Estimate propensity to be treated based on 1993 covariates
pre <- df[year == 1993]
ps <- glm(treat ~ log(revenue+1) + industry + county, family = binomial, data = pre)
pre[, w := predict(ps, type="response")/(1 - predict(ps, type="response"))]
df <- merge(df, pre[, .(firm_id, w)], by="firm_id", all.x=TRUE)

did_w <- feols(log(nox_emissions + 1) ~ did + log(employment + 1) | 
               firm_id + year, weights = ~w, cluster = ~firm_id, data = df)

# 6. Output
etable(list(Main=did_nox, Revenue=did_rev, Weighted=did_w))
```

------------------------------------------------
6. Expected Results
------------------------------------------------
Environmental outcome: A sizeable decline in NOx emissions among treated firms—on the order of 20–30 % within the first five years, deepening to ~40 % by year 10 as the cap tightens.

Economic outcomes:  
• Revenues – small negative or zero average effect (–2 % to 0) due to cost passthrough and compliance flexibility.  
• Employment – likely no significant loss; possibly slight gain in environmental compliance jobs.

Distributional effects: Larger, capital-intensive firms benefit (can trade cheaply); small untreated firms gain from cleaner air without incurring permit costs.

Unintended consequences: Spatial reallocation of emissions within the basin but limited evidence of “hot spots.”

------------------------------------------------
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (DID)
(Coded 1 = clearly satisfied, 0.5 = partly, 0 = doubtful)

C1. Parallel pre-trends visually & statistically verified ………… 0.5  
C2. No contemporaneous confounders specific to treated group … 0.5  
C3. No interference/spillovers across units ………………………… 0.5  
C4. Stable composition / no differential attrition ………………… 1  
C5. Robustness to alternative controls, weights, time windows … 1  

Total ≈ 3.5 / 5 → Reasonably credible but not bullet-proof; most concern lies with spillovers and parallel trends.

------------------------------------------------
End of Plan
